doc.title: Mike Longo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2019

title: Starting a solo and letting the music lead
summary: A solo needs a statement and corroboration; Stravinsky and Charlie Parker quotes support not trying to be different.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: If you had a student that just didn’t seem to have any direction to their improvising, like it was just a series of unconnected notes and phrases. Do you have something you can —

Yes. It has very much to do with how you start a solo. You must begin a solo with a positive opening statement followed by a corroborative statement, and then ontology takes over. And so you can’t play licks or anything after that because the music starts to develop on its own. So what usually happens is instead of making an opening statement the guys just start noodling, and so they’re [scats] that’s really what they’re saying. And so it’s really got to do with you’ve got to get a solo off on the right foot. And so if you don’t do that you’ll just be mumbling. And so I make my students have to make a statement and corroborate that statement and let the music take over. See Stravinsky said, “Music by its very nature is incapable of expressing anything. Music expresses itself.” And so when you hear people say, “I’m trying to do something different.” No man. That’s not the way it works. Stravinsky used to say, “There is no music that doesn’t come from tradition.” So you have to master the tradition and then the music takes you to another place. You don’t take the music. You can’t make music go anyplace. And so I’m a servant to the music. I do what — the music asks me to do something I do what the music — and so yeah my plans developed over the years because of that. I let the music tell me what to do. And so new direction is always coming out. And if you look at music history that’s really what happened. Somebody that’s trying to do something different is on an ego trip man. You dig? You don’t have to try to do something different. All you’ve got to do is play right. If you’re playing correctly — see there’s a big difference between
somebody who’s trying to do something different and somebody who’s not trying to do that and something different happens.

That’s a big difference. Charlie Parker — there’s a famous interview between Paul Desmond and Charlie Parker where he says, “How did you go about inventing this new music?” He said, “I wasn’t trying to invent any new music,” he said, “I was studying Lester Young and it just happened.” And so when the guy said whatever you read before about me having my own way, that’s why. I wasn’t trying to do anything. So what came out was I was just learning to play jazz properly, correctly. If you’re doing that and you’re mastering like there’s so much tradition in the guys that came before you, when you master all that the music takes you to another place. And if you’re playing properly your own voice starts to develop. So I have my own way of playing. Yeah.
